---
title: "Duodenal Adenocarcinoma"
format: revealjs
---


## Overview: Definition and Rarity
- Duodenal adenocarcinoma (DA) is a rare malignancy.
- Accounts for less than 1% of all gastrointestinal (GI) cancers.
- Incidence rate is less than 6 cases per million person-years.

## Overview: US Epidemiology (2018)
- Estimated 10,470 cases of small bowel cancer in the US.
- Resulted in approximately 1,450 deaths.
- Highlights the high mortality rate relative to incidence.

## Overview: Proportion of Small Bowel Cancers
- The duodenum comprises a relatively small portion of the small intestine.
- Despite this, DA represents the majority of small bowel adenocarcinomas (SBAs).
- Reported rates range between 55% and 82% of SBA cases.

## Overview: Histologic Subtypes
- Adenocarcinoma accounts for ~40% of all small bowel cancers.
- It is the most common histologic subtype of duodenal malignancy.
- Compared to lymphoma, carcinoid, and GI stromal tumors (GIST).

## Overview: Incidence Trends
- Epidemiologic studies suggest an increasing incidence of DA.
- Reasons for this trend are still under investigation.
- Highlights the need for updated clinical guidelines.

## Overview: Prognosis and Survival
- Prognosis for DA remains poor.
- 5-year overall survival (OS) is less than 50% even with curative surgical resection.
- 5-year survival rates drop to 15%–33% when all stages at diagnosis are considered.

## Overview: The Challenge of Rarity
- Rarity of DA is a persistent challenge to advancing treatment.
- Many studies aggregate DA with all small bowel cancers or periampullary tumors.
- Limits disease-specific data and targeted therapy development.

## Overview: Clinical Practice Guidelines
- Guidelines for SBA were only recently published.
- First by a French intergroup in 2018.
- Followed by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) in 2019.

## Presentation: Demographics
- DA demonstrates a slight male predominance.
- Most common presentation occurs during the 6th or 7th decade of life.

## Presentation: Delayed Symptoms
- Clinical presentation is often delayed.
- Tumors must grow large enough to cause noticeable symptoms before detection.
- Contributes to advanced stage at diagnosis.

## Presentation: Common Symptoms
- Bleeding is a primary symptom.
- Symptoms related to gastric outlet obstruction are highly common.
- Includes nausea, vomiting, anorexia, early satiety, and weight loss.

## Presentation: Nonspecific Symptoms
- Nonspecific or vague abdominal pain is commonly reported.
- Makes early clinical suspicion difficult.
- Often leads to delayed diagnostic workup.

## Presentation: Jaundice
- Patients may present with jaundice.
- Typically occurs if the cancer is located in the second portion of the duodenum.
- Due to obstruction of the biliary tree near the ampulla.

## Presentation: Asymptomatic Cases
- A retrospective Japanese study of 205 SBA patients evaluated asymptomatic cases.
- 64 patients (43.0%) with DA were asymptomatic at diagnosis.
- Highlights the hidden nature of early-stage DA.

## Presentation: Incidental EGD Findings
- 85.9% of asymptomatic DA cases were found via esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD).
- These EGDs were completed for unrelated reasons.
- Emphasizes the value of incidental findings.

## Presentation: Symptomatic Jejunioileal Adenocarcinoma
- In contrast to DA, jejunioileal adenocarcinoma presents differently.
- 47 patients (83.8%) were symptomatic at the time of diagnosis.
- Anatomical differences likely contribute to earlier symptom onset.

## Presentation: Consequence of Asymptomatic Progression
- Asymptomatic progression leads to high rates of late-stage diagnosis.
- High rates of unresectability at the time of initial presentation.
- Underscores the need for better early detection strategies.

## Presentation: Late Stage at Diagnosis (Japanese Cohort)
- 24.2% of new DA cases were found to be Stage 3.
- 20.8% were found at Stage 4 disease.
- Demonstrates the burden of advanced disease at presentation.

## Presentation: Western Countries vs. EGD Surveillance
- In Western countries, EGD for gastric cancer surveillance is not routine.
- The risk for late presentation of DA may be even higher than in Japan.
- Lack of routine upper endoscopy delays diagnosis.

## Presentation: Resectability Rates
- A significant proportion of DA patients do not proceed to curative intent surgery.
- Systematic review indicates 29% of DA patients receive palliative treatment only.
- Curative options are lost due to late presentation.

## Presentation: French Cohort Study
- Recent prospective cohort study from France evaluated resectability.
- Demonstrated that less than 60% of SBAs were resectable at diagnosis.
- Confirms the global challenge of surgical candidacy.

## Presentation: Periampullary vs. Extra-ampullary
- Periampullary tumors often present earlier than extra-ampullary tumors.
- Likely due to earlier biliary or pancreatic duct obstruction.
- Slightly greater percentage of periampullary lesions are resectable at presentation.

## Gross Pathology: Macroscopic Appearance
- DAs appear as circumferential "napkin-ring" type masses.
- Can also present as polypoidal fungating masses.
- Growth patterns influence the onset of obstructive symptoms.

- **Panel A**: Macroscopic photograph of a resected duodenal adenocarcinoma.
- **Panel B**: Microscopic image of a duodenal adenocarcinoma.
- Visualizes the typical gross and histological presentation of the tumor.

## Gross Pathology: Tumor Size
- Median tumor size at presentation is approximately 4.0 to 4.6 cm.
- Reflects the delayed clinical presentation and prolonged asymptomatic growth.

## Gross Pathology: Size and Resectability
- It is important to note that tumor size may not be a primary factor in resectability.
- Vascular encasement and metastases are more critical determinants.
- Large tumors can still be resected if localized.

## Pathogenesis: Multistep Process
- The pathogenesis of DA is incompletely understood.
- Available data suggest a multistep process of malignant transformation.
- Progresses from an adenomatous polyp to carcinoma.

## Pathogenesis: Acquired Mutations
- Driven by acquired mutations in key oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes.
- Similar to the adenoma-carcinoma sequence seen in colorectal cancer.
- Highlights the genetic basis of the disease.

## Pathogenesis: Key Genetic Drivers
- Mutations in SMAD4, KRAS, TP53, ERBB2, and TGFBRII are reported.
- These act as drivers in the malignant transformation of preexisting polyps.
- Targetable pathways for future therapeutic research.

## Pathogenesis: Villous Adenomas
- As with colon cancer, villous adenomas harbor the most malignant potential.
- High-grade dysplasia in villous architecture increases carcinoma risk.
- Justifies aggressive surveillance of villous lesions.

## Pathogenesis: Distinct Genetic Profile
- The genetic profile of SBA is distinct from both gastric cancer and colorectal cancer.
- Despite some overlapping mutations, the molecular landscape is unique.
- Implies that treatments for colon cancer may not perfectly translate to SBA.

## Pathogenesis: Chronic Inflammation
- A role for chronic inflammation is suggested in DA pathogenesis.
- Perhaps secondary to exposure to intestinal carcinogens.
- Leads to the accumulation of somatic mutations and eventual malignant transformation.

## Risk Factors: Lifestyle Factors
- Body mass index (BMI) is suggested to be associated with increased DA risk.
- Alcohol intake is also linked to higher risk.
- Smoking remains a significant risk factor for DA development.

## Risk Factors: Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)
- The most important hereditary syndrome contributing to DA.
- Patients harbor a germline mutation in the APC gene.
- Promotes polyposis and tumor formation in the colon and duodenum.

## FAP: Duodenal Involvement
- DAs will develop in nearly all patients with FAP.
- The periampullary segment of the duodenum is most commonly affected.
- Requires rigorous lifelong upper GI surveillance.

## FAP: Post-Colectomy Mortality
- DA and desmoid tumors are the leading causes of death in FAP patients.
- This applies specifically to patients who have already undergone colectomy.
- Shifts the clinical focus to upper GI and extra-intestinal manifestations.

## FAP: Spigelman Classification
- FAP patients with duodenal polyps are staged from 0 to IV.
- Based on histologic and macroscopic findings.
- Guides the frequency of endoscopic surveillance and surgical intervention.

## FAP: Progression to Stage 4
- Progression to Spigelman stage 4 is often slow.
- One group found a 22.4-year median time to progression from first EGD.
- Allows a window for intervention but requires long-term commitment.

## FAP: Surgical Intervention for Polyposis
- Patients with advanced stage Spigelman polyps are offered duodenal resection.
- Goal is to precede progression to invasive carcinoma.
- Balances surgical morbidity with cancer prevention.

## FAP: Effectiveness of Screening
- Screening to prevent DA in FAP patients has been found to be variably effective.
- Not all patients benefit equally from standard surveillance protocols.
- Highlights the limitations of current endoscopic monitoring.

## FAP: Danish Study on Screening
- Study of 304 FAP patients by a Danish group.
- Found significantly improved survival after screening-diagnosed DA.
- Survival was 8 years vs. 0.8 years for symptom-diagnosed DA (p<.0001).

## FAP: Limitations of Surveillance
- Despite screening benefits, some patients still develop late-stage DA.
- Not all FAP patients have preceding Spigelman stage IV polyposis before cancer.
- Cancer can arise de novo or from lower-stage polyps.

## FAP: Upstaging on Final Pathology
- Patients undergoing resection for Stage III/IV polyposis are frequently upstaged.
- Final pathologic analysis often reveals invasive duodenal carcinoma.
- Demonstrates the difficulty of distinguishing severe dysplasia from invasive cancer endoscopically.

## FAP: French Series on Surveillance
- Large French series: 437 patients undergoing over 1900 endoscopies.
- Over 20% of patients undergoing surgery for advanced polyposis were upstaged to adenocarcinoma.
- Confirms that surveillance is not fool-proof.

## FAP: Extent of Surgical Resection
- Extent of resection depends on the number and distribution of polyps.
- Limited resections may be performed if endoscopic removal is impossible.
- Tailored to the individual patient's polyposis burden.

## FAP: Need for Second Resection
- Patients undergoing limited resection may require a second, more radical resection.
- Indicated for recurrent late-stage polyposis.
- Highlights the progressive and relentless nature of FAP duodenal disease.

## Risk Factors: Lynch Syndrome
- Lynch syndrome confers a risk of DA, though lower than FAP.
- Requires aggressive endoscopic surveillance.
- Associated with DNA mismatch repair (MMR) deficiencies.

## Risk Factors: Lynch Syndrome Statistics
- Relative risk (RR) of DA is estimated to be 100-fold the general population.
- Lifetime risk of developing DA is approximately 4%.
- Justifies inclusion in Lynch syndrome screening protocols.

## Risk Factors: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome
- Also confers an increased risk of DA.
- Risk is significantly higher than the general population.
- Requires vigilant monitoring of the entire GI tract.

## Risk Factors: Peutz-Jeghers Statistics
- Risk of DA estimated to be between 1.7% and 13%.
- Hamartomatous polyps can undergo malignant transformation.
- Underscores the need for multidisciplinary management.

## Risk Factors: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)
- IBD is thought to be associated with an increased risk for DA.
- Chronic inflammation drives somatic mutations.
- Similar to the well-known risk of colorectal cancer in IBD.

## Risk Factors: IBD Retrospective Data
- Retrospective study of over 9,000 patients with IBD.
- Significantly increased risk of small bowel cancer (RR = 3.70; 95% CI 1.23–11.1).
- Confirms the statistical link between IBD and SBA/DA.

## Risk Factors: Celiac Disease
- Case reports and epidemiologic studies suggest celiac disease increases SBA risk.
- Chronic mucosal inflammation and villous atrophy contribute to malignancy.
- French guidelines recommend evaluating celiac disease in DA patients.

## Diagnostic Workup: Initial Studies
- Varies depending on patient symptoms and individual risk factors.
- Evaluation of any duodenal mass requires a tissue diagnosis.
- Once confirmed, complete staging is mandatory.

## Diagnostic Workup: Staging Objectives
- Determine the resectability of the primary lesion.
- Rule out evidence of distant metastases.
- Staging is based on the TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system.

## Diagnostic Workup: Endoscopy
- Tissue diagnosis and location relative to the ampulla are obtained via upper GI endoscopy.
- Essential for planning the type of surgical resection.
- Allows for direct visualization and biopsy.

## Diagnostic Workup: Cross-Sectional Imaging
- CT or MRI used to assess resectability.
- Crucial for ruling out metastatic disease and vascular involvement.
- Standard of care for preoperative staging.

## Diagnostic Workup: Radiologic Findings
- Intraluminal exophytic mass.
- Intramural mass with ulceration.
- Central necrosis can also be present in larger tumors.

## Figure 63.2: Radiologic Imaging of DA
- **Panel A**: Barium swallow showing narrowing of the duodenum secondary to DA.
- **Panel B**: Abdominal CT image demonstrating a mass in the second portion of the duodenum.
- Illustrates classic imaging modalities and findings.

## Diagnostic Workup: Resectability Criteria
- Potentially resectable tumors show no evidence of major vascular encasement.
- No distant lymphadenopathy.
- No distant metastases.

## Diagnostic Workup: Surgical Planning
- If a segmental resection is planned, endoscopy must confirm the tumor's relationship to the ampulla.
- Proximity to the ampulla dictates the need for pancreaticoduodenectomy.
- Critical for avoiding positive margins.

## Diagnostic Workup: NCCN Laboratory Studies
- Guidelines indicate lab studies should include CA19-9 and CEA.
- Tumor markers assist in baseline assessment and future surveillance.
- Not diagnostic on their own but prognostically useful.

## Diagnostic Workup: Evaluating Comorbidities
- Patients should be evaluated for celiac disease and/or IBD.
- Depends on the overall clinical picture and symptoms.
- Important for comprehensive patient management.

## Diagnostic Workup: Molecular Testing
- DNA mismatch repair (MMR) or microsatellite instability (MSI) testing on tumor tissue is recommended.
- Identifies patients who should be tested for Lynch syndrome.
- Opens doors for immunotherapy if MSI-High.

## Diagnostic Workup: French Guidelines
- Include colonoscopy to assess for synchronous lesions in all DA patients.
- Ensures no concurrent colorectal malignancies are missed.
- Reflects the field defect theory of GI malignancies.

## Treatment: Surgical Therapy Overview
- Surgical resection is the strongest predictor of long-term survival in DA.
- Only curative intent surgery offers a chance for prolonged survival.
- Requires careful patient selection and preoperative staging.

## Treatment: Survival with Resection
- For invasive adenocarcinoma, most series report a 5-year OS of ~40%.
- A 2018 meta-analysis of 6,438 patients showed a 5-year OS of 36%.
- Median survival was 31 months in the pooled analysis.

## Treatment: Curative vs. Palliative Intent
- Two meta-analyses compared curative intent surgery to palliative treatment.
- Curative intent increased 5-year OS to 46%.
- Palliative treatment only yielded <1% 5-year OS.
- Emphasizes the paramount importance of surgical resection.

## Treatment: Endoscopic Resection
- Only patients with dysplasia or carcinoma in situ are candidates for endoscopic submucosal excision.
- Invasive disease requires more extensive surgical intervention.
- Endoscopic therapy is strictly limited to early, non-invasive lesions.

## Treatment: Extensive Operations
- Any patient with invasive adenocarcinoma requires segmental resection or pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple).
- Technical details are complex and require specialized centers.
- Goal is R0 (microscopically margin-negative) resection.

## Treatment: Optimal Extent of Resection
- Continues to be a subject of debate.
- Rarity of cancer limits high-quality comparative studies.
- Balances oncologic clearance with surgical morbidity.

## Treatment: Periampullary Tumors
- Uniform agreement on the necessity of pancreaticoduodenectomy.
- Required to achieve negative margins and adequate lymphadenectomy.
- Segmental resection is oncologically inadequate for periampullary DA.

## Treatment: Extra-ampullary Tumors
- Retrospective series and SEER database (1998-2010, 1,611 patients) evaluated resection types.
- Demonstrated NO survival difference between pancreaticoduodenectomy and segmental resection.
- Applies to extra-ampullary tumors that do not invade the pancreas.

## Treatment: Confounding Factors
- The equivalence of resection types for extra-ampullary tumors holds true even after controlling for confounders.
- Includes extent of disease and patient comorbidities.
- Supports parenchyma-sparing surgery when oncologically safe.

## Treatment: Lymphatic Drainage Patterns
- 3rd and 4th portions of duodenum drain into the small bowel mesentery.
- NOT via the pancreaticoduodenal lymphatic basins.
- 1st portion often drains to the pyloric nodes.

## Treatment: Anatomic Considerations
- Understanding lymphatic drainage is critical for surgical planning.
- Lymph node metastases are a major prognostic factor.
- Resection must encompass the appropriate nodal basin.

## Treatment: Impact of Lymph Node Metastases
- MGH and Mayo Clinic series showed drastic survival drops with node positivity.
- MGH: 5-year OS decreased from 65% to 25%.
- Mayo: 5-year OS decreased from 68% to 22%.

## Treatment: Meta-analysis on Lymph Nodes
- Meta-analysis of 11 studies (654 patients) confirmed the prognostic impact.
- Node-negative disease had a 65% 5-year survival vs. 21% for node-positive.
- Prognostic importance remains after correcting for tumor size, grade, and stage.

## Treatment: NCCN Lymph Node Recommendation
- NCCN guidelines recommend evaluating at least eight lymph nodes.
- Ensures adequate staging of small bowel and duodenal cancer.
- Prevents understaging and guides adjuvant therapy decisions.

## Treatment: Extent of Resection Principles
- Based on the tumor’s location with respect to the ampulla.
- Must ensure the ability to obtain an R0 resection.
- Must allow for adequate lymph node sampling based on drainage patterns.

## Prognosis: Perineural Invasion
- MGH series identified perineural invasion as the most powerful independent predictor of survival.
- 5-year OS was 56% WITHOUT perineural invasion.
- 5-year OS dropped to 19% WITH perineural invasion.

## Prognosis: Histologic Subtypes
- Extra-ampullary DAs are characterized by morphologic and immunophenotypic traits.
- Gastric type (50% of cases).
- Intestinal type (37% of cases).
- Pancreaticobiliary subtype (5% of cases).

## Prognosis: Intestinal Type
- Has the most favorable prognosis among subtypes.
- Generally expresses CDX2, MUC2, and CD10.
- Mimics colorectal adenocarcinoma biology.

## Prognosis: Gastric and Pancreaticobiliary Types
- Gastric-type tumors express MUC5AC and MUC6.
- Pancreaticobiliary subtype behaves more aggressively.
- Subtyping may guide future targeted therapies and prognostication.

## Neoadjuvant Therapy: Rationale
- Several small retrospective series evaluated neoadjuvant therapy for DA.
- Demonstrated occasions of pathologic complete response.
- Can convert unresectable lesions to resectable ones.

## Neoadjuvant Therapy: Mayo Clinic Series
- Evaluated 10 patients with unresectable DA.
- Conversion to resectability achieved in 9 patients.
- 3 patients showed complete or near-complete pathologic response.

## Neoadjuvant Therapy: NCCN Guidelines
- Recommend neoadjuvant therapy for locally unresectable or medically inoperable DA.
- Requires close monitoring for conversion to resectable disease.
- Offers a potential curative pathway for initially hopeless cases.

## Adjuvant Therapy: Rationale
- Many patients are offered postoperative adjuvant therapy.
- Based on the premise that DA shares features with colorectal cancer.
- Adjuvant therapy benefit is well established in colorectal cancer.

## Adjuvant Therapy: NCCN Guidelines (Stage III)
- Recommend adjuvant therapy for patients with positive lymph nodes (Stage III).
- Standard of care for node-positive small bowel adenocarcinoma.
- Aims to eradicate micrometastatic disease.

## Adjuvant Therapy: NCCN Guidelines (Stage II)
- Consideration of adjuvant therapy for Stage II disease with high-risk features.
- High-risk features include T4 tumors, poorly differentiated histology.
- Also includes lymphovascular/perineural invasion or tumor perforation.

## Adjuvant Therapy: Chemoradiation
- Noted as a treatment possibility for Stage II or III disease.
- Specifically indicated for patients with positive or close surgical margins.
- Aims to improve local control in the duodenal bed.

## Adjuvant Therapy: Extrapolation from Colorectal Data
- NCCN acknowledges recommendations are extrapolated from colorectal cancer literature.
- Proven efficacy in the specific context of SBA is lacking.
- Preferred regimen is enrollment in a clinical trial.

## Adjuvant Therapy: French Guidelines
- Similarly adopted from colon cancer treatment paradigms.
- Recommends adjuvant chemotherapy for Stage III disease.
- Consideration for Stage II disease with T4 tumors.

## Adjuvant Therapy: Mixed Retrospective Data
- Retrospective data supporting these practices is highly mixed.
- Systematic review of 6 studies (148 treated vs. 263 untreated).
- Showed NO significant benefit (48% vs. 46% 5-year OS, OR 1.14).

## Adjuvant Therapy: Second Systematic Review
- Pooled outcomes for 607 patients with DA.
- Did NOT demonstrate an overall survival benefit for adjuvant therapy.
- Hazard risk (HR) = 0.96, 95% CI 0.75–1.23.

## Adjuvant Therapy: National Cancer Database (NCDB)
- Contrasting retrospective study using NCDB data.
- Showed increased median OS for adjuvant chemotherapy in Stage III SBA.
- 42.4 months vs. 26.1 months without adjuvant therapy.

## Adjuvant Therapy: Chemotherapy vs. Chemoradiation
- Comparison of adjuvant chemotherapy alone vs. chemoradiation.
- Demonstrated NO benefit for the addition of radiotherapy.
- Even in patients with positive surgical margins.

## Adjuvant Therapy: Limitations of Retrospective Data
- Analyses often aggregated patients receiving ANY adjuvant therapy.
- Were not stratified by specific chemotherapy regimens.
- Limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions on optimal drug combinations.

## Clinical Trials: The BALLAD Trial
- Ongoing international prospective, randomized study.
- Aims to clarify the benefit of adjuvant therapy for Stage I–III DA.
- Known as the Benefit of Adjuvant Chemotherapy for Small Bowel Adenocarcinoma (BALLAD) trial.

## BALLAD Trial: Objectives
- Objective 1: Compare disease-free survival (DFS) in adjuvant therapy vs. observation.
- Objective 2: Compare DFS between fluoropyrimidine-based therapy with or without oxaliplatin.
- Designed to provide Level 1 evidence for SBA.

## BALLAD Trial: Randomization Strategy
- Uncertain value of chemotherapy: Randomized to observation vs. LV5FU2.
- Certain benefit of chemotherapy: Randomized to LV5FU2 vs. FOLFOX.
- Stratified based on risk and stage to optimize trial design.

## BALLAD Trial: Primary Outcomes
- 3-year disease-free survival.
- Overall survival.
- Results are highly anticipated to change global treatment paradigms.

## Current Standards Pending BALLAD
- Until BALLAD results are available, current standards apply.
- Neoadjuvant therapy for select unresectable patients.
- Adjuvant therapy for resected disease with aggressive biology, positive margins, or node metastases.

## Patterns of Disease Recurrence: MGH Series
- Evaluated 83 patients with DA treated between 1982 and 2010.
- Recurrence documented in 37 patients (44.6%).
- Median follow-up time was 14.5 months.

## Patterns of Disease Recurrence: Locoregional vs. Distant
- MGH series showed an approximately equal proportion of recurrence sites.
- Locoregional: 16 of 37 (43.2%).
- Distant: 17 of 37 (47.2%).
- Both: 4 of 37 (10.8%).

## Patterns of Disease Recurrence: Norwegian Series
- More recent series of 69 patients treated from 2000 to 2015.
- Over 80% of first disease recurrence was distant.
- 29 of 36 patients (80.6%) experienced distant failure.

## Patterns of Disease Recurrence: Most Common Site
- For both the MGH and Norwegian series, the liver was the most common site of distant recurrence.
- Highlights the hematogenous spread pattern of DA.
- Suggests a need for better systemic control.

## Patterns of Disease Recurrence: Clinical Implications
- High rate of disease recurrence and associated poor prognosis.
- Underscores the importance of ongoing, collaborative research.
- Focus must be on improving systemic therapy for more durable disease control.

## Summary: Key Takeaways
- DA is a rare but highly lethal malignancy of the small bowel.
- Early detection is hampered by vague symptoms and lack of routine screening.
- Surgical resection (R0) remains the cornerstone of curative treatment.
- Adjuvant therapy is widely used but lacks Level 1 evidence pending the BALLAD trial.
- Multidisciplinary care and clinical trial enrollment are strongly encouraged.
